An exponential moving average updates a running value using a fixed fraction of the new observation.
The update has the same algebra for different objects, but its interpretation depends on what is being averaged.

## The update and its object {#ema}

An EMA of values $v_t$ uses

$$
  m_t=\rho m_{t-1}+(1-\rho)v_t,
  \qquad 0\leq\rho<1.
$$

Older observations receive geometrically decaying weights, with an initialisation contribution until it decays or is corrected.
The averaged object matters: model weights, a teacher's weights, losses, and action predictions are different objects.
[DINO](../../literature-review/vision/dino.qmd) averages teacher parameters.
[ACT temporal ensembling](../../literature-review/action/act.qmd#temporal-ensembling-uses-a-common-target-time) combines predictions for a common execution time and uses its own age convention.

## How past values contribute {#weights}

For a fixed decay $\rho$, unrolling the update gives

$$
  m_t=\rho^t m_0
  +(1-\rho)\sum_{j=1}^{t}\rho^{t-j}v_j.
$$

The latest value has weight $1-\rho$, and each additional step into the past multiplies its weight by $\rho$.
The initial value still contributes $\rho^t m_0$.
Thus, initialisation and the identity of the time index matter when comparing two averaging procedures.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: expand the recurrence"}

Substituting the previous update once gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  m_t={}&\rho^2m_{t-2}\\
  &+\rho(1-\rho)v_{t-1}+(1-\rho)v_t.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Repeating the substitution back to $m_0$ yields the visible sum.
The data weights sum to $1-\rho^t$, while the initialisation contributes the remaining weight $\rho^t$.

:::
